title: Exclusive Interview with Andre Szmyt
text: Welcome back to Cleveland Browns Daily brought to you by Bally Bet, an official sports betting partner of your Cleveland Browns. And oh baby, couldn't be happier than to be joined by Browns kicker Cade York Andre Szmyt. Andre, as you stand here, smiles on your face, full of confidence as you should be. Can you believe that a year ago you were about to start your NFL career and kicking your first regular season game. And here you are now. >> I can't believe it. Time's truly flown by and what a different situation it is this year than than last. >> No competition in training camp. You go out there have a great training camp, great preseason, all of that. How are you feeling going into this one? And just from And you dealt with a lot, obviously, last summer. How different do you feel going into this season than you did a year ago? >> Yeah, I think obviously a lot more confident. I mean, been in the stadium, played in these in these different stadiums, with these different teams. So, I feel I feel confident. I feel ready to go. And I put a good preseason, like you said, together in training camp. And comfortable with the guys, too. I worked with them all off season, so feel good. >> Yeah, bringing back that battery, you, Rex, Corey. That's How helpful is that? How big of a deal is that? >> Yeah, it makes a huge difference. I mean, just having the familiarity with Corey and Rex, like it's it's good to have those guys back. >> How is your swing right now? How do you feel about that? It's a lot like golf, and I know you've been taking up golf, getting more into it, getting in the sim in the summer, obviously, not right now. But how How is the swing and how do you feel like you've been hitting the ball? >> It's good. I feel like I'm hitting the ball well. And I was kind of feel like I was in a groove at the end of last season, so I kind of wanted to see where I was at there and just kind of mimic that and translate that into camp and the preseason. And I feel like I've done so. And just want to carry it into the season. >> Do you believe in jinxes? >> I do. >> Okay, good. So, you know that you have not missed a kick in the regular season or preseason since we were in New England last year. Last time that you missed a kick. >> Yeah. >> What clicked for you after that kick? And then we're going to talk about why that kick miss kick turns out wasn't your fault. New New information has come to light. >> Oh, really? >> But go ahead. Yes, but yeah. What do you think clicked for you after that? >> Uh, I think just like getting comfortable and like settling down and getting into like a rhythm. Um, not making the moment bigger than what it is and just kind of feeling you go out there and you're like in a in a good in a good rhythm. I think that's the only way I can put it is just like you feel like your your operation is smooth and the tempo is good and you're making clean contact and it almost feels like you don't have to think much about it and you just kind of go out there and do. >> That's important in golf, too. You can't can't think too much. >> Exactly. And that's like what I was trying to get to. Now I kind of start that earlier in the season. Just getting a good rhythm and that's what I was trying to do training camp and and preseason, you know, working with the guys getting as comfortable as possible to kind of start off in that kind of flow state. >> Yeah, let's go. How good did it feel in Chicago to knock a 50-yarder in at Soldier Field? >> Yeah, good. Another one, too. We had one in in December, another 50-yarder, too. So >> Two for two on those, yeah. Pretty good. All right, so let's go back to New England. So there was a a report that came out today. I don't know if you've seen this or not. >> No. >> But and I don't know if they still do but we're going to say for the sake of our discussion that they still do this. There was a study that was done that the Patriots made 9.4% more of their kicks in their stadium than their opponent. >> Hm. >> The biggest margin in the league outside of that was like 4%. So it is a huge statistical outlier. So what they would do is on the board where you were kicking, if you're kicking this way on that scoreboard, they'd show the the the uprights but like off center. >> So that if you were looking at your uprights they'd be a little to the left. If you're on the left hash it was a little to the left. If you're on the right hash it was a little to the right. So you could look through see that. And they had the flag they were showing actually a mirror so that the flags are going the opposite way of the flags on the field. >> Interesting. I didn't even notice that. >> [laughter] >> notice it? Well, we're going to say that perhaps they were doing this. So that was one of the things they did. When their kickers kicked they just kept it like black. >> And so that was one of their little tricks. Little tricks of the trade there. >> Fascinating. >> Belichick, listen, they were not afraid to to get those out. Do you even see See scoreboard? Should be illegal. >> No, no. I don't focus on the scoreboard. I just try to keep my eyes at the uprights and like pick a spot where I want to hit through through them. So, I didn't even notice that. >> Okay, good see. There you go. >> Those are the ones that feel good. >> No, we're going to go and we'll blame it anyway. All right, take us through All right, Browns are down now. We get into the 30 and you know that this is either going to be an extra point or a field goal. Take us through what you do on the sideline to the time you go on the field and just walk us through your whole the Andre Smith experience as I would call it. >> just in the net. It's very kind of a lonesome position. I'm just by myself in the net. As soon as we get into field goal range, I try not to hit too much into the net and fatigue myself out. >> It's kind of like once you hit a couple of field goals and you're like, all right, I'm good. I got it. >> Yeah, usually I'll just wait till like we're on like third down and then like I'll hit one maybe second down I'll hit one into the net. It like overcoming and like making yourself stronger to be in that situation that you are built for it. And so like telling myself like I know I'm meant to be here. Like I know I'm talented enough to do this. Like kind of the let the doubt side of your head and just put your faith in in God and yourself that you you're you're meant for it. >> And so kind of all the other noise, all the other like week ones in the past, you know, look forward to the future. text: This is a huge year for T.J. Hockenson, both for what he means to the Vikings and what it means to his own career. >> You are Locked On Vikings, [music] your daily Minnesota Vikings podcast, part of the Locked On Podcast Network, your team every day. >> What's going on, everybody? Welcome to the Locked On Vikings podcast, where we're always trying to learn something new. Today's episode is brought to you by Cal Sheet. For a limited time, download the Cal Sheet app and use code locked on to get $10 when you trade $10. Today on the show, I want to talk about three Vikings who have a lot riding on this year. Vikings who need to either step up or live up to the expectations that they've set on themselves. This is a conversation about circumstance, not necessarily a prediction. Those players are T.J. Hockenson, who is in a contract year and has quite a bit riding on what's going on. Jordan Addison, who is also in not a contract year, but a contract negotiation year. They've got his fifth-year option next year, but he's going to be paying getting paid the big big bucks or not next year, and this season will have a lot to do with that. And Dallas Turner, who has been pegged by a lot of people, myself included, as a breakout candidate. And if that breakout doesn't come, things could sour pretty quickly. But if it does, he could become a core pillar of the Vikings for years to come. There's a ton riding on this season for those three guys. Big names, core players on the Vikings. And the first one is T.J. Hockenson. Of course, T.J. Hockenson in the last couple years, it's been a little disappointing ever since his injury in 2023. He comes back from 2024, he's clearly not the same, not quite himself. 2025, uh everybody's production goes down as the offense falters. So, as if you missed it, as part of the Vikings cap nego uh cap navigation this offseason. They had T.J. Hockenson take a pay cut. And to get T.J. Hockenson to agree to take a pay cut, Hockenson requested that they void out the rest of his contract. Say, "Okay, I'll get paid less this year, but you got to let me go afterwards. And I'm going to go to free agency, and I'm going to going to negotiate myself there." That is an act of betting on himself. And if he were negotiating in free agency right now, it would be pretty rough. He hasn't had a 500-yard season since the 2023 season where he got injured. He's older. Um you know, there was a viral clip from last season of him running a route that looked kind of chunky. And so, his reputation is as low as it's been in some time. And to rescue that reputation, he needs to have a good year in 2026. What we define as a good year in 2026, I don't like to do it based on like yards or whatever. But there's a few things that are required of him for the Vikings offense to succeed. I always think about the way that we would see all of this going on once we have the benefit of hindsight. 5 10 years from now, everybody's out of the league, you're done, and the whole thing has turned over. We're talking We're debating over a totally new version of the Vikings. How will we look back on this and tell his story? And depending on how 2026 goes, I could see two very different answers to that. If Hockenson is ho-hum again and quietly exits, has a little retirement tour, does a couple of cheap years somewhere, doesn't really make his money anymore, retires, it's going to go down as, "Okay, Kwesi kind of overpaid for a guy, didn't quite get what he wanted from it. It was like, okay, but ultimately washes away in the mediocrity of the last few years of the Vikings." If he has a good year, what happened in '24 and '25 with Hockenson immediately gets dismissed with the excuses that I brought up before. Those excuses become valid as soon as he proves that they were that those those stat lines were not indicative of his play. And I'm just talking about receiving here right now. As a blocker, that's another important thing. This is the thing about tight ends. Football is not a series of one-on-one matchups. I say that a lot. We we often think of it in that way, right? Broadcasts will highlight this edge rusher versus this tackle or this corner versus this receiver. That's not how football is played. That's not how football is planned. That's not the strategy anybody comes up with. Everybody's try They're trying to all be more than the sum of their parts. And so, this is not Hockenson can't run a route and get open against a linebacker that's clamping him up in man coverage. A lot of what Hockenson does in in the the passing game and what he does in the blocking game is going to be dirty work. That's what tight ends do. I looked up his routes on TrueMedia, just his route distribution over the Kevin O'Connell era, over his time in Minnesota. And the vast majority or the the two runaway majority routes are outs. This is PFF's charting, so that counts both short outs and deeper outs like, you know, 10-yard out or whatever as part of like flood concepts. And hitches, over the ball, choice, that kind of stuff. And I think depending on what choice does, they'll chart it as an out or an in. Um so, there's a fluctuating amount of like what they called in routes, but point being most of a tight end's routes are going to be shorter. This is the big lumbering blocker guy. We're not sending him all the time on, you know, we're not trying to streak him down the field and have him beat anybody on a deep post or anything like that. Um there is some of that. I'll get to that in a sec, but the point is a tight end's receiving role is more about showing up in the right place when you're supposed to be there and less about do you have the wiggle to beat that linebacker or you know, get open against that nickel corner or you know, what are you going to do? Hockenson will use his size to get open a lot. Most tight ends will run routes that way. Like these are not the most agile guys, right? They're all like 280 lbs. So instead, they'll just kind of bully their way through somebody, get to the spot they're supposed to get to, try not to slow down, break, and say, you know, I'm going to get away from you unless you hold me. And Hockenson is no different in that way. But really it's about showing up where you're supposed to be. And attacking the right hole in the zone and something like that. Like running a 5-yard hitch doesn't have a huge skill differential. The best tight end and the mediocre random, you know, third-string tight end are both just going to run a 5-yard hitch and they're not going to look all that different. The consistency with which you catch it and how well you can muscle through a catch and stuff, which is something Hockenson's not been great at, that might be a more differentiate differentiating factor. But the point is tight ends are about um precision. It's about doing the right thing. Blocking the right guy from the right angle and doing all that, which Hockenson, for the record, is fine at. I'm going to talk mostly about receiving today. Again, I think of Jason Witten's uh I I I think a lot about like the end of these tight ends' careers. Jason Witten's. He was insanely unathletic at the end of his career. I mean, by the time he was done, people talked about it as like dad running, right? People would make fun of him. Dak Prescott trusted that, and so you could still dump the ball off to him and he would go do his thing. He's not running away from anybody, and they never asked him to run away from anybody. It was still a useful thing. And that is the role of a tight end. Add that to blocking and the versatility of that role. If you can do that and be a good blocker, you're a great tight end and everybody's going to be really happy with you. That's a valuable piece that enables a whole bunch of other things. If you run your route properly and don't get open, you still lure the defender you were supposed to lure and the other thing is opened up the way the concept is designed and the way it expects you to. That's why football's not a series of one-on-ones. A lot of times it doesn't matter if you win yours. You're sacrificial. Your your route is just meant to clear somebody out or it's just meant to to influence a linebacker or bring somebody down out of the deep part of the field so we can do something else deep. That said, the next two routes that are most common for Hockenson are deep crossers and go routes. Those are the deep routes and that's the thing that Hockenson needs to show a propensity for. Not getting open on them, but being fast enough where those are the uh where where those are threatening. That's cardio, right? That's somebody just running down the field and you have no expectation of them getting open, which is why you give the tight end that because if you're going to ask anybody to run a route without getting open, how about the guy that's that's halfway an offensive lineman? Have him do it. But he's got to be fast [clears throat] enough for that clear out to still work. When you put a clear out into a route concept, you're trying to deepen a safety. You're trying to bring somebody out of the coverage that has to respect that route. So, if that safety can not respect the speed and say, "I'm just going to stay where I'm at. If you do blaze by me, I can always turn around and catch up cuz I'm faster than you." If he's not threatened by that speed, that route concept won't work and that was a problem with T.J. Hockenson in the past. They They did that with like C.J. Ham in the past, trying to give the sacrificial route to the the least prolific receiver. And then if that guy's not fast enough, the whole thing doesn't work. They kind of get a little cute on themselves sometimes in that way. And deep crossers work the same way, right? It's all about spacing and timing. Have I gotten 30 yards down the field and over the ball at the same time Justin Jefferson did so that we can cross over each other and stress out their coverage. If I can't get there in the same time, and you know, they'll often have this spaced out where the path to that for Jefferson's a little longer so that he does have a little time to catch up, but you can only do that so much. If you're so slow that you're not getting there at the right time, these concepts don't work out and then you're no longer as trustworthy in the past concepts and it's like, "Okay, you're just kind of Captain Checkdown." And you're just going to be that guy and it's going to be a 400-yard season and then that's fine. That's what it's got to be for Hockenson. On those deeper routes, the speed has to be there. title: Seahawks Press Conference - September 5, 2026
text: Back in our usual uh What was it? Wednesday? Wednesday setting. Uh excited for the week. Guys are in great spirits. Kind of going back to the process, you know. Just so it's We just got to be great at the things we can control at this point. You know, games at the beginning of the year are um are really just about how well we can play our style of ball and and trust that uh that the results kind of take care of themselves, but really excited about playing at home to start the start the year off and um off we go. Look forward to today's practice. I know we're going to have a lot of injury questions, but uh So, not going to answer them. So, you can ask if you want, but I won't answer them. >> When it comes to actually having an opponent this week, what's the joy that you get from game planning and truly diving into that? >> Uh it's it's it's good. It's a good change of pace. It's a good change of pace. Again, the first first game of the year is is a little tricky, you know, like you you can't be you don't you don't want to fall in the trap of applying, you know, last year's things that you see too much to what's going to happen this year, you know, um teams will grow and evolve and change and there's different personnel and on both sides, so. I think our focus is trying to trying to do the things that that we do that um our guys can go play the best they can and also try to apply as much pressure as you can as well, but um understanding how the game goes, there's going to be some things that we're going to be required to make adjustments in game cuz there's inevitably there's going to be things that happen that um you haven't prepared for. >> Like this will be your not very much weight put in like a Super Bowl matchup. >> Oh, of course yeah, you're going to you're going to watch that and try to understand how they attacked you in different ways and things that you did and um but again, you know, just you can't be you can't be all in on on certain things at this point. >> Like this will be Brian's first opportunity to call plays in a regular season setting and it maybe thinking about when you had your first regular season game getting to call plays and what advice do you have for him going into a situation like this? >> Yeah, I think um it's about I think it's with like with the rest of our players, it's trusting our training, trusting the preparation. Uh definitely you know, you feel the but I mean shoot, I still do that, you know, you still feel you're you're always going to you're always going to feel um there's you know, whatever. Is it anxiety? Is it uh excitement? Um those things are natural. It means you care. It means it matters to you. I hope our players feel that, but it's also you know, when you when you do when you do have those feelings, understand like hey, you know, we're still playing a football game that we prepared for and um take a deep breath and go let it rip and let's rock and roll. >> You talked all the way back in like OTAs about sort of put the Super Bowl in the right place, running it forward, all that. Now that you've been through training camp, preseason, and your team's here week one, how do you feel like the players handled that? >> Yeah, they they have done a great job. They've done a great job. I think um I think trying to put it in perspective, too, that like we're we're beginning this journey. This is this is um a you know, it's it's awesome that we get the it's week one and it's it's exciting and there's context behind it and everything, but it's also uh the first step of this journey as well. So, you know, whatever comes out of the game, then we're going to have to no matter what, we're going to have to grow and evolve to be you know, to become the team that we want to become by the end of the season. So, but it it's it's uh it's cool. I mean, how many opportunities do you have to you know, start the year off at home, drop the banner, all that stuff. I mean, that that's that's kind of that put that in the bucket of the the time the singular things that happen that you can, you know, take the have that moment that you work for. That's why the guys work so hard is to have moments like that. So, we definitely want to respect that when it when it happens. >> You guys last year first game, offensive plan seemed a little different than the rest of the year, only one play action pass. Maybe not your best fast balls, I guess is using your parlance. How do you kind of prepare differently for to get the season started on a different foot this year? >> Um we haven't really we haven't talked about our approach last year. I think we're focusing on our approach this year. I think the the point remains that there's going to be things that happen in this game that that we really like and there's going to be things process-wise that we're going to want to adjust. Um hopefully it's not so much on the latter, but if we're doing it right, we're definitely going to find things that that we want to be able to evolve from moving forward. So, I don't think you can worry about that. I think I think you got to focus on let's put the best plan in place, which I feel great about our plan up to this point. And uh make the necessary adjustments throughout the week and then and then uh go dial it up the best we can. >> And how do you approach a situation like you mentioned where unique you guys played this team last year, you played them the first game this year. How do you get the players to kind of see this as a new match up and not just a repeat of a game that you already won? >> Well, there's a lot of new players involved. So, that that makes it simpler to to get that message across. Context has changed. I mean we haven't we haven't really hasn't really been a topic of conversation. There's things that It's been a long time between the two games and I I think both both teams would tell you that we're different versions of you know, of who we are. So, in that way like it does help the message of hey, we're a new team. Sure the Patriots feel the same way and and uh we're focused on like on doing what we need to do in this game, you know, to uh to make it come to life. >> Back to the the question of like running forward, how have you sensed that the players have handled the stuff that like can potentially come with winning a Super Bowl and complacency and all that? How How have you felt like they've handled that? >> I've I feel like our guys have done a great job. Um I feel like if we would have sniffed it out, we would have addressed it. But I feel like when we've gone out on the field, our intent's been really good. I mean we we you know, are there days that we felt like we probably could have grown more or could have done a better job? Yeah, but I think that's just that's what happens. Um but I think that's just like our mentality of like we're always kind of searching for ways to to make what we do better, you know. >> The process, Mike. The process, Mike. how besides the scout team and running the scout plan and game plan, how has the process for the players changed from training camp to this week? >> Uh well, we we've been in a kind of quote-unquote in-season schedule here for maybe 2 weeks. What did you see that allowed them to be so effective? >> They're also pretty good on third down, too. Um I think overall they're just a really they're they've been a really explosive offense. So, and and it comes in different ways. It comes in the run game. you know, in the core and on the perimeter, it it's come in the uh in the action game. It's come off schedule, it's come off on outside lane throws, it's They do a really good job. They they changed a lot of their receiving core this off season. How does How does the addition of A.J. Brown and Romeo Dobbs maybe create some different challenges that you guys have to deal with that you didn't have in February? >> Well, that's another example of hey, there's there's new personnel on both sides of the ball and you can you can guess all you want on how they're going to use, you know, their new players um based off of what they've done in their past and how they've utilized players in their offense in years past, but you know, at best that's a educated guess, you know, so you know, we're going to have a a way that we expect to that trying to guess where, you know, try to have have an understanding of where they're going to be and then we have to do a great job in the game of understanding how they've been utilized and how we're structuring our coverages to, you know, combat that. Have you had any more contact with them >> Yeah, we have few a few times. Um it's been great. It's been great conversation. I know John's probably been in more contact with them than than I have. So, I think regardless of, you know, win or loss in the first game, I think it's all about just us preparing as a team and us showing up as the way we want to show up. You know, in terms of like how we play our style of football and things like that. And you know, we'll let the outcome be the outcome, but we obviously all want to win in this league and that's our goal is to win again this season, but you You I don't want to take the loss as, you know, the end of our season cuz it clearly turned it around for us last year. >> How much lighter do you take the challenge of doing this again and how rare it is to go back-to-back and go all the way climb the mountain again starting over? How much of that alone is a challenge for guys like you and DeMarcus who've been around the league a while? >> I mean, I will say it's definitely a challenge. Um, you know, especially com- coming off of a Super Bowl. Um, you know, people are going to play us differently. Um, teams are going to see us as the Super Bowl champions, defending champs, and they're going to probably going to play harder against us than they would other teams. And, uh, you know, I have a great example in my father-in-law, uh, Ronnie Lott, who's done it before, and he talks about how hard it is and how much, uh, we have to forget about the last season and focus on now. And, uh, that actually gives me a lot of hope because I see that in the building. Um, like I've been saying the whole time I've been up here, um, everybody's done a good job of like handling that success and just looking forward. Like nobody's talking about what we were last year. We're all focused on how can we get it done this >> Do you explicitly talk to him about that or did he bring it up to you? >> Yeah, he brought it up to me, uh, just like shortly after the Super Bowl. Um, you know, he realized how many of our guys were like stay- staying on the team. Um, you know, I was talking to him about, you know, D-Law coming back and me coming back and all these other guys, uh, that are vets. And, you know, he talked about how hard it is to, uh, to repeat. And, um, you know, that was part of what he told me that's hard about it is, you know, guys look to that last season that they just had instead of looking forward. And, uh, you know, we're not doing that around here. >> a chance to talk to any of the players that were on the 2013 team that won the Super Bowl and then came back the next year and they managed to get back to the big game, obviously. But, have you had a chance to talk to any of those guys about that? >> Yeah, actually I have a good relationship with like Kam Chancellor and, uh, Richard Sherman. And, uh, they pretty much all tell me the same thing you know, Ronnie told me. So, it's, uh, clearly, you know, different, uh, phases of football, uh, different times. um but it's all the same thing. It's like uh just focusing on what's ahead and and not looking back. >> Leo, speaking of looking ahead, what do you think is coming this year for Byron? >> I mean, he's just one of those players that I've seen steadily grow since he's gotten this league. Um he's a quiet, humble kid, and he's just always looking to grow as a player. Um you know, he's just super stout and dominant in the run game, and uh I think he's just been growing in more and more as a pass rusher. >> It seems like you guys are going to use him at three more this year. Like what what should that do to allow him for his pass rush to come alive a little bit more instead of eating the double teams all the time? >> Yeah, for sure. I think uh being able to rush at the three technique is going to open up some opportunities, and uh just him being um you know, in the system for 3 years now, just more experience. Uh he's been able to learn from a lot of vets in his D-line room, and uh he's he's a sponge. Um he takes up a lot of information, and uh he's always willing to learn and and grow. So, I think he's going to just continue to do that. >> You just mentioned you're in year three in this system. Mike's defense is obviously not the simplest one for guys to come and learn. Where have you seen kind of what that experience has done for you guys? A lot of you guys have been in this defense 3 years now. >> I mean, it allows us to play faster. Uh just being under the same system, under the same uh coach for this long, we we understand the coaches' expectations, we understand expectations from each other, and we understand uh where we got to be and the expectations of the defense. And uh by doing that for, you know, long enough with the same group of guys, you start to learn each others' tendencies and understand what it takes to get the job done, and um I think it just allows us to play faster, uh especially at home. We got to, you know, work on different verbal communications, nonverbal communications, and um you know, when you're in the system for this long, uh it allows you to do that a lot faster. >> Have you seen anything different out of Sam Darnold going against him in practice this year from, say, this time last year at all? >> I haven't, and I say that in a good way. Sam's been the same guy since he's come in the building and uh he's the type of guy who's just working. He's the first one in, last one out. You know, he's a great leader. He's just always watching film. You know, when we're on the plane and we have time to just mess around, goof around and hang out with each other, he's sitting there, you know, studying film and trying to work on his game. And you know, that's something I love about Sam is you're going to get the same person with him no matter what day it is, no matter if we just came off of a win or a loss. You know, regardless of what's going on outside of football for him, he's going to show up as the same guy every day. >> What about the offense as a whole? I mean, that last year Sam was new. A lot There's a lot more newness last year scheme-wise. Does it feel like the offense has been ahead of what you saw last year in camp? >> Yeah, definitely the way they attack the ball. You know, they get lined up fast. They have a lot of motions. You know, they move [clears throat] the tight ends and fullbacks and stuff like that a lot. It makes it hard on our defense. So, there was a lot of good competition throughout camp. And you know, I'm definitely looking forward to seeing how they can continue to grow. >> Every contender needs a deep defensive line. What are you anticipating from Riley Mills this year? >> I mean, I expect Riley to step up a lot this year. You know, he had a great Super Bowl game, which was like his first game back. But even before that game, you know, he was injured all season. So, you can see a different hunger and drive in him. You You know, you could tell that he was down a lot of the of the time last year and he's just ready to do whatever it takes to be out there on the field with us. >> A lot of defensive coaches head coaches in the NFL have played the game. What about Mike has allowed him to be a guy that did not play at the highest level and still is a defensive head coach? >> What What was the question? >> So, a lot of the defensive head coaches out there like Demeco Ryans are guys that played defense in the NFL. Mike's not one of those guys. What What allows him to command respect and and lead you guys from a defensive side even though he did not play the game? >> I think it's, you know, just his work ethic, his determination, the way he chases edges. I've talked about this before, you know, he he preaches chasing edges and we see that in him. He's always trying to find ways to exploit an offense, put us in the right position, allow us to play fast and free. And you know, he's definitely got the respect of everybody in the building. You know, especially on the defensive side, he came in and we all just knew that he he understands how to call defenses and he understands how to exploit offenses. So, I think it doesn't really matter if you played the game or not. If you're good at doing that consistently and always find a new ways and chasing edges, then you're going to get the respect from the guys in the building. >> What's going on? >> Did you obviously didn't see the offense in the preseason at least the starting offense, but from what you've seen in camp and all the way up to this point, just how do you feel like you guys are preparation wise, you know, year two with Sam, similar scheme and all that? >> Yeah. I think a lot of guys in our offense have, you know, played some some snaps uh in the NFL at this point and um we would have been happy to play honestly in the preseason had we played, but coach and the other guys we felt like, you know, it was we got a lot of good reps during camp. Um so I think, you know, don't make it any bigger than what it needs to be, you know, it's first week in the NFL. Uh obviously a big deal, but you know, we played football on uh not on a Wednesday before, but on any other NFL game we we we've played, so. >> Are you fully back now, ready to >> Yeah. Yeah, feeling good. Um you know, I think you're always have a nick here or there, uh nature of the business, but um I feel very good. I feel very confident um mentally and physically uh with where I'm at and really just excited to play my brand of football um for the Seahawks. >> You played last year with injury and in this game even. Um and now you've gone through your off season and rehabbing. How do you feel differently than you feel at the end of last season? >> Um I just feel uh honestly I would say, you know, hopefully it's not anything really physically for me like I I once I step on the field and cross these white lines like I don't really want to feel any type of different. Um but mentally I think I've taken strides just to learn the game and know my role and uh know the flow of the game. But, you know, it's week one. I think you should feel hopefully as good as you can. And uh for my case that that's the way I feel. >> Do you anticipate the tight ends being used a little bit differently this year? How much new newness was there that you needed to learn versus kind of going back to last year's offense? >> Yeah. Um I think for myself and the rest of the tight ends uh any opportunity that we can, you know, get a bunch of us on the field um and being personnel groupings that has tight ends is a great thing for us. And I think new new positions maybe um depending on, you know, what guys we have out there, what tight ends we have out there. You have to know the position that you're playing. Um and for myself I think, you know, I'm a you know, a tight end that's going to, you know, remain at tight end. So, for me it's kind of not not necessarily too different. Um but obviously the more tight ends we can get out there at full back, at Z, at F, whatever it is. Um we we're up to the challenge in our room. >> AJ, we've seen Elijah have a pretty solid preseason. What what are you expecting from him in year two for him? >> Yeah, I think just another step. Um I think for myself, you know, year one to year two is definitely uh a difference for myself. And I think same thing for Elijah. Um and we've seen that already in the preseason. So, just any opportunity he has to make a play um you got to just go make it and then one will follow the next. Um and you just take off from there. So, it's going to be a good year for him and he's already off to a great start with the with the momentum he has from preseason. >> How has the relationship with Brian Flurry evolved with you guys from kind of day one when you showed up to now? >> Yeah. I think know his personality a bit more now, you know, just on a coach to player relationship, you know, just having those conversations inside and outside of football. Um but I think throughout the year you kind of learn your play caller as well. I think for any player um the more plays that you make in a game uh I think the play caller is going to have a bigger appetite to you know, call more plays for you, so for any guy on our team, I think you know, it's just taking advantage of opportunity and um but uh we're we're comfortable with coach Flurry you know, calling it and uh feel like you know the scheme is is uh in a good place. >> With Bobby being out and you talk about how tight ends a lot of times get used in the fullback spot what's the difference in terms of being off off the line and hitting your blocks and targeting when you're you're in a fullback kind of role, H-back role than then on the line tight the line? >> Yeah, I think it just kind of changes the angle uh maybe the speed that you're you know, you're attacking the blocker. Um but I think once you get into contact, you definitely want to remain on that same target that you might have had um whether you're on the ball or off. And um Brady's done a great job. Um Dissly mixes in mixes in there as well and same with Elijah and I can you know, be back there as well, so um I think it's just a bit of a different angle and a a different downhill approach than when you're on the ball. >> Back to Flurry, I think we've only talked to him a couple times since he got hired. What what is his personality like and is there some Clint to him? There's some character there? >> Yeah. Yeah, I think you know, you guys probably reason you guys only talked to him a few times kind of you know man of few words. Um he's about you know, he's about ball, about his business and similar to Clint in that aspect, you know, where he um can be a little bit you know, more reserved um but then once you get to know him, definitely you know, learn his personality. Um but I think the biggest thing with coach Flurry is you know, he just wants to do a great job the for the 12s and for the Seahawks. Like he knows the capabilities of our offense, of the players that, you know, sit in this room, and um you know, he's he's excited for the opportunity. >> And in this style offense, how important is it to have a number of tight ends that really compliment each other with the different things they bring to the equation? And how does that impact your game? Like if you have Elijah out there with his ability to stretch the field vertically. >> How important is that in an offense that makes tight ends such a focal point for single moving around? >> Yeah, no, very important. I think uh the biggest thing for us in this offense and the way the Seahawks play the ball play football is, you know, our tight ends we have to be able to run at our tight ends, away from our tight ends, whatever it is. We're not flipping our hips in the hole. We're going to go, you know, take the block to you if you're at D end. And um that's something that I really pride myself in is I'm going to, you know, bang with whoever is out there and not be passive about it at all. Um and I think having Elijah or Dissly or myself or Brady to stretch the field as well, you know, can take the top off, get you on a safety, get you on a linebacker, and um you know, really really present, you know, versatile versatile um pictures to a defense. >> What do you think about getting your first action of the year and and opening night? Do you also envision the 12s, the banner drop, the environment, the vibe? >> Oh, yeah. Um really excited for the 12s. I love, you know, the crowd. I feed off the energy since I've, you know, began playing football. Banner's going to be special. For me, I'm ready to turn the page though. Like Super Bowl was awesome. Definitely a sick moment, but like it's over with. It's in the past. We still love it. But like I'm good. Let's go play some some new football. >> What's the key to turning that page? >> Um I think, you know, we we've we've we've lived it and um you know, that first hit, you know, the Patriots don't care, you know, that about that banner going up. The rest of the 31 other teams, they don't care about it. So, um it's time to go. It's time to turn the page and the banner will be cool, but um it'll be there, you know, tomorrow and the day after that as well. >> They did that. Here's a clip of Hard Knocks the leadership council, and you might have been the youngest guy in that room, third-year guy. What does it tell you that or what does it mean to you that like the team sees you in that kind of leadership role in only your three? >> Yeah. Yeah, you know, I've been in that room for, you know, some time now, so it's not really different for me, and I think um that's just who I am as a person. Um I was a captain in college and whatnot, and um whenever my team needs me to to be vocal or be myself, um I'm, you know, always there to do that, and I think I just want to be myself, and coach Mike loves me for that, my teammates love me love me for that, so being in those rooms, I'm able to just be myself and and voice my opinion about, you know, what I think the team might need. >> What do you like about the way Mike does that in the leadership council and kind of gets feedback from you guys on how certain things are done? >> Yeah, I think it's it's cool because, you know, you have a collection of guys that um can kind of take the temperature of the locker room um and the player perspective and speak on behalf of the players as well. Um and Mike's great cuz he'll listen to that and um you know, really apply those things to whatever it is that we're doing. >> Did you watch all of the Hard Knocks, and if so, what did you think of it? >> I did not. I saw a bunch of clips on um you know, Twitter, um but it sounds like they did a great job. You know, we have a bunch of awesome people in this building and uh have played great football here, so what's not to like? >> Is Flurry down with the uh the barnyard? >> When can we see that? >> Yeah, we we should see it um you know, whenever whenever the time permits, but I don't think it's going anywhere. >> Good. >> All right. Thanks, guys. >> I'll do it. >> Mhm.

title: What Aaron Donald's Return Says About the Rams...
text: I'll start with you first cuz you gave the little lean back. How are you feeling? What's your take because we do have to save time to get to Hard Knocks tonight, so we won't make this long. >> I I I'm fine with it. Like I I I didn't think he looked I This is going to sound I I'm going to say this and it's going to sound really stupid in a couple of weeks. I I don't think he looked that like Aaron Donald when he was when he was practicing on the tape they took. I mean, he obviously he moves very well for a man of his size, but there was always that something like absolutely terrifying about Aaron Donald. And and I didn't see terrifying when he was running through the pads and all of that. So, I've no doubt that when he gets on the football field and maybe gets the the blood flowing, he'll still be a dynamic force. And of course, Miles Garrett's going to be uh taking up a lot of attention on one side, isn't he? So, that's presumably what's really appealed to him to to come back is that he's maybe not going to be double-teamed as much as before, but I don't know. The Rams are either going to just be so much better than everybody else and and win this thing and we're going to have to just take our hats off to them and say well done and uh enjoy it. Or the other the opposite's going to happen. And I I don't know. I Maybe this is just wishing it into reality. I just don't know whether this kind of like superstar team thing works. I We've We've been here before with other teams. Like the Eagles had like a superstar team and it just imploded and look at all of this stuff that they're doing. Matthew Stafford's nearly 40 years old and he's he's had bad backs in the past and it and he's like one injury-plagued season away from all of this being for naught. Cuz I'm not I'm not being funny. I do not see Stetson Bennett or Ty Simpson coming in and carrying them to the Super Bowl. I So, I don't know. I'm not I'm not saying that I think the Seahawks are going to go and smash them twice and that they're going to pick sixth overall or something next year, but I equally I'm not quite ready to give them the crown and the throne just yet. >> Yeah, Brian, we have people, not just Rob, but any any sports fan really on all ends of the spectrum with this. We're hearing crazy things. We're hearing people that are like, I don't know yet. Like, where do you fall on this scale right now with this news? >> I'll just say this, AB. I think it's very fitting that Aaron Donald comes back because it's pretty emblematic of that whole Rams franchise's mindset. They're front-runners. And if would Aaron Donald be coming back if they didn't trade for Myles Garrett, if they didn't have an MVP quarterback, if they didn't have all this stuff going on, if they didn't have a home game for the Super Bowl again 5 years after they had one like 6 years, whatever it is. Like I think it says a lot about the mentality of that whole organization that this guy who's an excellent Hall of Fame level just game wrecker is like, oh yeah, it would be fun to just never lose and have such an unfair advantage. I'll play that. I'll play that. I'll get off my couch for that. Think about that compared to the way the Seahawks are wired. Like, you've got guys that came here without any promise of any of that happening and bound together as brothers and and teammates to do something really special last season. And so it still will be the same test. Like when if, I guess, if things don't go well at any point, if they do have injuries, if they do have suspensions, if they do have some losses, how does that team handle it? Like, that's that's what I'm going to be wanting to watch because it's one thing to come back. It's another thing to endure. So, let's see. Let's see. But look, they've got a lot of room for error with the amount of talent that they've got. They could They could probably lose Matt Stafford for five games and still win three or four of those just by holding other teams to not many points. So, it's I I don't think it's we should get it twisted. It's an unprecedented amount of talent on one team. And I'm really curious to see what happens with it. [snorts] >> Can Can Can I just throw some fanales out there as well? This is going to be really interesting to see how they start cuz they've got to go to Australia and they're bizarrely doing this like, "Well, we're going to go in the night before, play the game, and come back." It doesn't really work that way though, does it? Cuz Australia the time difference is so huge. The I I don't think you can just sort of fly in and fly out again. >> Time travel. Time travel, Rob. >> So, and also, Shanahan always seems to have, apart from the game that it really mattered in the NFC Championship, seems to have the Rams' number. So, that's going to be an interesting first game. They then play an upstart New York Giants team after that with with a a proper head coach in charge now. So, we'll we'll see and then they've got to come back from Australia and play that. So, that's interesting. They then go to Denver and Philadelphia in their next two games. And then the the game after that is at home to the Bills. That's That's a very interesting first five games of the season. And from what Brian was saying there about how do they react if they lose a couple of What if they They could easily lose a couple of of those games and it would be fine. Like they're just close games, good games, good contest. Josh Allen has an amazing game. Sean Payton has an amazing Whatever. But they could lose a couple of those games. It'd be interesting to see how they respond to that. And you know, they could have a difficult start. I mean, if they blitz through that schedule as well, we might as well just give them the crown if if they can stay healthy cuz that if they can win all of those games, they are legit. But that's a tough start for them. >> Well, hey guys, we're going to be talking about this for a long time because it's not just when week one comes and we'll figure it out

title: We NEED to Talk About the Jason Myers Situation...
text: So, Rob, it's probably uh not a crazy take to have. But on the topic of scoring, uh we do have to talk about the Seahawks special team scoring because that has been something that did not cross my mind once headed into the preseason, especially uh because of the performance, especially throughout the season, but also in the Super Bowl that we saw from Jason Myers going five for five. Like, he could have been he could have easily been a Super Bowl MVP depending on how the the end of the game went. But when you look at this specialist group, like same group. Um, you know, Brian, is there anything that we should be concerned about with the missed field goals from the kicker this this preseason? >> Uh, I'm the wrong person to ask, AB. I know it's it's uh part of the job description, but as much as I'm able to separate emotion from bias and data and all sorts of other things with analyzing football and the Seahawks, I can't do it with with kickers. [laughter] I I'm so frustrated when kickers miss kicks. >> New segment for you. Ready? New Hawk Blogger mornings. Okay, just get out on the field and start kicking field goals and just talk and do it at the same time. You know what? This could be a new segment. >> So, >> when Rob goes to Seattle, you both can do it together. Rob's a holder, Brian's kicker. >> I think I think I'd be good up to about 40 still. >> Oh, wow. Okay. >> Yeah. I I I'm not going to say >> Were you a soccer player? I was. Yes. >> Okay. Well, there we go. >> So, yeah, I like I'm not going to say I could be an NFL kicker because there's no way I could be an NFL kicker and I couldn't do what those guys do, but I I could hold up in a in a little field day, but honestly, I just um there's something about it for me. So, so to answer your question directly, I do think it's something to be concerned about. anyone that's played any sport that requires the coordination of a sequence of events in order to execute like whatever you're trying to do. Shoot a shot, swing a golf club, swing a tennis racket. There's like all sorts of things that kind of sequence together. You can see that Jason Myers is out of rhythm. Like it's just his sequence is off. And it can just come right back the next day like you change one thing and it's all just nails. or it can just like play with your mind and you cannot find it. And right now like that that field goal at the end of the Chiefs game was about the worst possible [laughter] thing to leave in all of our minds because it just that that was not a good kick. So I don't know. I hope it works out. I admit I have been really critical of the Seahawks not ever bringing in a younger kicker, a cheaper kicker when the league is getting 70 yard kickers from 70 yard kicks from rookies like all over the place now for league minimum and the Seahawks are paying a guy like eighth or ninth highest cap space cap hit on their team. I I I wish that they had brought in a little bit more competition there. Uh but we'll see. Well, hopefully this all turns out well and he has a year just like he did last year. >> Yeah, it's a very interesting situation because of what we saw last season from him really saving a lot of games and so uh you want to be able to lean back on that and obviously it's a a huge mental position as well. Rob, what are your thoughts on this? Well, I I think definitely the it's cause for concern and and before this game I was saying, look, let's just slow the roll a little bit here because yeah, he's had a bad couple of games, but it's preseason and I remember last year the special teams, you know, people were talking about is Jay Harbaugh good enough and there was all sorts of kick coverage issues in preseason and ended up having the best special teams by a mile in the league. So, sometimes you kind of just get through it, but then when he missed the extra point, you're thinking, here we go again. And then, you know, I was pleading you again, stupidly stayed up till 4:00 in the morning to watch that absolute hell hole of a fourth quarter. Uh it was just awful. Um and and watching that and I thought when he's got that kick, I thought this is why I've stayed up cuz I want to see him nail this kick and then and then get to sleep. I didn't sleep for about 20 minutes after watching that kick because I'm just sort of thinking in my head. We're gonna be talking about this, you know, as a fan base and as a media now and >> and Annabelle's going to ask me about it. >> Well, no, no, I think it's a it becomes a thing because if he nails that kick, you can go, well, he's not had a great preseason, but at least he got that game-winning kick at the end. Okay, great. But then it just now you're sort of counting all the kicks he's missed and you start to worry a little bit. Now I do think he deserves a chance to put things right against New England and hopefully he will. But when I'm sat in that stadium a week tomorrow and he's lining up for his first kick, whether that's an extra point or a field goal, me and 60 odd thousand others are going to be thinking, "Please get this." And that's not really where you want your kicker to be. The only sort of thing that's given me any kind of comfort at the minute is I've been looking around the league and I who was it like the Jets have been rotating kickers and you know I saw I tweeted this uh yesterday that uh Adam Shfter tweeted with kicker Tyler Loop, what a name that is by the way, Tyler Loop experiencing an uneven preseason, the Ravens signed Jake Moody to their practice squad. And I'm thinking, yeah, there's always somebody worse than you, isn't there? So, the guy who replaced the wrong at kicker who blew the AFC uh North title last year for the Ravens is is had such a bad preseason that you're now bringing Jake Moody in for a look see. Like, that's worrying. And it goes to show that while it's certainly the case that the Jaguars have found a good young kicker and the Cowboys have have recently paid their kicker and there there's one or two others that are doing the rounds. Uh the Niners have found this quite challenging to the point they might have finally settled on somebody. The Rams I believe what was it the thicker kicker is it they brought in last year and even he missed a kick against the Seahawks and that could have won them the game in week 16 and could have won them the homefield advantage. he missed that. And now you've got the Ravens struggling like this that there are one or two others as well that that do not have uh good kicking situations. It feels to me like the the league's kicking situation is as in flux as it's ever been really. Um, so I'm just hoping that we don't have to join those other teams in kind of scrambling around for options and that Jason Meyers can get back to his near Super Bowl MVP level performance because after he had that iffy game in week 18 against the Niners where he missed a couple of kicks, I think I'm right in saying he was eight of eight in field goals and 11 out of 11 for extra points in the playoffs. Didn't miss a single kick. >> Right. Well, that's the hope. That will be the hope for week one. And I even remember going back to last season talking about the Patriots specifically. They had rookie kicker Andy Borggales and he missed some crucial kicks in the first two weeks of the season. And I believe it was when they were down in Miami and he missed a a pretty bad kick and then was able to get it back later in the game and help them win the game. And I believe he got a game ball and Ray Bull speaks very positively about that and his team had his back. And so you can just imagine like the the dialogue and the discourse and like how your teammates and coaches are talking to you, the the body language that they're giving like that matters especially for that position. Uh whether you are a veteran or you're a rookie and it turns out like you saw the trajectory that Andy Borgal had that season being a being a huge factor for them. Uh, so that is definitely something to keep tabs on. But more to come on the Seahawks collective and it is time for our prize picks lineup of the week. Uh, here it is. We got all Pats and all Hawks to get you ready for their Wednesday night game. And guys, fantasy scores. What else would you want? This is like a dream for so many of our twelves. So, uh, Brian and Rob, what are you going to go with here? We got both QBs. title: The Good and Not So Good About Australia
text: I've been in Australia for three days, which makes me an expert on the continent and its culture. Here's the good and not so good about it. The good, the accent. It's not like Scotland where people allegedly speak English, but the accent is so thick it sounds like another language. I can understand Australians, and their accent is fun. Every vowel is an adventure. It will start with one sound and then slide to a completely different sound in the same syllable. A knife isn't just a knife, it's a knife. And no isn't just no, it's no. These sliding vowel sounds are called diff thongs, and Australians can't get enough of them. Neither can I, apparently. Two, the coffee. It's as good or better than the coffee on the West Coast, and it's not served with half and half. They serve it black, sort of like an Americano, or they make something called a flat white, which is kind of like a latte. Both are delicious. Three, meat pies. They're everywhere. You can get a mass-produced microwaved 4 and20 meat pie at a stadium, slather it in ketchup, and eat it in 30 seconds and you won't die. Or you can get a really tasty one from a bakery and enjoy it. I had the 4 and20 version. It wasn't great, but it did the job. Four. Pot in a Parma. The pot is a small 9 oz glass of beer. Small so it doesn't get cold. And a Parma is the go-to pub food in Australia. It's essentially chicken parmesan with some ham on it. So it's like chicken parm cordon blur. It's way better than it should be. Five. Australian rules football. As my Australian friend Steven Moss put it, there are 36 punters varying 5'8 to 610 running a half marathon while constantly punting and punching the ball. It's a hand pass with tackling from any direction. Punt through the sticks more than the other guys to win. All of these players are deadly accurate at punting an oblong ball with either leg. They're ambi punters. I said that and they tackle each other. It's an old game that meshes unusual skills with toughness and violence. I'm hooked. Six. Melbourne cricket grounds. It's where the 49ers and Rams will play. It seats about 100,000 people and the field is a giant oval that's roughly 200 yard long. We don't have fields like this in America. It looks like a battlefield from medieval times. And they sell meat pies here. Seven. Patrick Dangerfield, one of the best players on the Jalong Cats, which essentially is a suburb of Melbourne and is home to my favorite team in the AFL since I learned about the sport two days ago. This guy is 36 years old and he still kicks ass. He took over a game two nights ago against the Carlton Blues by scoring five goals. This was the best performance I've ever seen in my two days of watching the sport. The not so good one, the driving. Sometimes I could see myself moving to Australia and loving it in lots of ways. It's like California, similar climates and sensibilities, but people drive on the left side of the road here, and I could never get used to that. I would crash my car. I would never even try to learn. I'm too old. I couldn't trust my instincts on the road. Even when I walk on the sidewalk, I create problems because everyone here walks on the left side of the street. I walk on the right side while looking at my phone. I keep bumping into extremely polite Australians. Two magpies. They're these gorgeous black and white birds, and they will swoop down and ruin your day if you're not careful. That's what I've been told. They were nice to me, but I gave them distance. Three, the metric system. I never know the temperature outside or how much weight I'm lifting at the gym or how fast I'm running on the treadmill. Yeah, I work out. Four, the burritos. As I said before, Australia and California have a ton in common. Mexican food is not one of those things. I went to a Takaria yesterday that said it had mission style burritos, so I was intrigued. text: We've got a 49ers update from the easternmost tip of mainland Australia. That's right. In this direction, 8,000 miles, all water back to San Francisco. Well, maybe a few islands, like Hawaii, on the way. But, as the 49ers get ready in Melbourne, making all of the appearances that the Rams aren't, I'm working my way up the coast of Australia. Now, speaking of this ocean and this direction, the 49ers actually have their own bottled water brought in from Hawaii, 13 pallets worth, across this ocean. I am now at Cape Byron. Shout out to the Byron back in the Bay Area, who occasionally flies the 49ers and flew us over the Golden Gate Bridge. But, Cape Byron features a beautiful lighthouse built between 1899 and 1901 that was last in operation in 1989. Obviously, a 49ers Super Bowl winning season. You know what else happened on the way to the Super Bowl for the 49ers in 1989? They beat the Rams 30 to 3 in the NFC Championship game at Candlestick Park. There's been a lot of talk about Anaheim Stadium right now, since the owner of the Rams, Stan Kroenke, just bought the Angels. Remember that back in the day, the Rams played in Angel Stadium down in Anaheim, and it was enclosed, and I call it Kmart Candlestick because it was like a knockoff of Candlestick Park with the full enclosure and the seating to accommodate both baseball and football. Well, fun fact about that stadium, Joe Montana never lost there. So, we're here to talk about Brock Purdy and how he's one of the elite quarterbacks and better than Matthew Stafford in a very key way, especially as we're starting to handicap this matchup between the 49ers and the Rams. Take a look at this. It is efficiency per dropback from a clean pocket versus efficiency per dropback when a quarterback is pressured. Purdy from a clean pocket, number two efficiency in the entire NFL. The sample is 2023 to 2025. You see at the top of the clean pocket chart is Jared Goff, but what happens when Goff is pressured? Drops from number one all the way down to number 28. Purdy though, when he's pressured, drops only from number two to number four. See where Matthew Stafford is at. Number seven when it comes to EPA from a clean pocket, down to number 22 when it comes to EPA from pressure. So, I mean, the big question is can the 49ers get some pressure on Matthew Stafford? They weren't able to do that effectively last season, even in the game that they won. They weren't really able to get pressure on anybody after Nick Bosa got hurt last off season though. When Stafford is pressured, he is not nearly as good as Brock Purdy. The data is clear. He's not as mobile as Purdy. The thing that makes Brock Purdy truly elite is that he can play out of structure. Stafford is relying on McVay's structure. He's relying on Puka Nacua. He's relying on things working around him. Purdy isn't necessarily reliant on that, which is why he's been so damn good for the 49ers over the course of the past several seasons. So, it leads us to the quarterback matchup. 49ers Rams, one QB who's still very efficient even if he's pressured, another QB not nearly as efficient when he's pressured. Now, the Rams, at least on paper, obviously have greater capability of creating pressure than the 49ers. Even had to fly a new hedge rusher across this ocean to help pick up some of the slack. So, the advantage that the 49ers have since the Rams are obviously stronger on paper defensively is an edge at quarterback, at the most important position when it comes to evading pressure. Now, that's before we get to talking about the travel advantage. And I have now been here long enough, and this is a fairly strenuous physical activity. I'm talking on video while I'm climbing up from I was down at at sea level just a few minutes ago. So, I'm testing my physical exertion, and I will say that I feel back to my normal self, but it took a swim in this ocean for me to get there. I swam back up further north earlier today when I was along the Gold Coast. Now, we're in a much more northern California-like area. I mean, this almost reminds me a little bit of the Cliffs of Moher as well. But, I will it took me I'll say about 30 hours or so to feel physically normal, and I had it good when it came to the flight. 9 and 1/2 hours of sleep was one of the biggest adrenaline rushes I've gotten in a while when I woke up and saw that we were only 90 minutes away from this beautiful coast. The Rams are going to travel with lay flats as well. And I'm sure that some of their players will also get 9 and 1/2 hours of sleep, but I don't know if the odds are good that the entire roster will get that kind of sleep and even with the well-executed sleep that I got, melatonin-fueled, even with that considered, I didn't feel physically right until maybe 30 hours after landing, and the Rams will be playing a football game 24 hours after landing, and I'm venturing to say that most of them are not going to be jumping in the the ocean here. I don't think that the Rams would be very happy about that. A lot of the signs say that there are a lot of sharks, but I think they're actually more shark attacks in Northern California where I swim, so we'll we'll take that as a point of pride. Anyway, I don't see how the Rams can possibly get a leg up with their particular approach of traveling at the last minute. I don't see how the 49ers can be disadvantaged by this. I think it's only potential benefit for the 49ers. And when you look at the Rams and you say, "Okay, maybe this team has a more complete roster than the 49ers." Well, you also have to counterbalance that with the entire travel and rest equation, which is obviously extremely unique in this scenario. You have to counterbalance that, too, with the main position, the most important position. And the 49ers have Brock Purdy at that one, while the Rams have an aging Matthew Stafford. Now, Stafford was undoubtedly extremely efficient last season, but he also had a top-tier run game. And he also had a top-tier line. How much of the Rams operation will stay elite here in 2000 26? And how much of that can the 49ers cut off at the root? Can they improve their run defense to the point where Stafford cannot rely on a top-five run game any longer to ensure that he stays protected? Can the 49ers find different weaknesses with the Rams? They've been watching the 13 personnel tape all off-season to figure something out. Yeah, I mean these are the questions that all need to be answered. Now, for the game week preparation update, and it's very one-sided because the 49ers are the only team that is going to practice here in Australia. They've got a formal big practice on Monday, then one on Tuesday, and then one on Wednesday. They've been knocking some of the jet lag and the rust and the aches off over the course of this end of week {slash} weekend Australian rules football for the 49ers at the Melbourne Cricket Ground, which by the way is going to have a very skinny-looking NFL field on it. This is going to be crazy. The Melbourne Cricket Ground is the largest stadium in the Southern Hemisphere, but they're going to put the 49ers and the Rams on an NFL field. The goalposts have been shipped across multiple oceans here to Australia, and the 49ers had a chance to check out the Melbourne Cricket Ground where they will be playing. They also had a chance to to check out a soccer match or football, as I guess they would call it here in Australia. And where they're at, and I'm on my way, I'll be there tomorrow. It's it's much cooler as I work my way from the north to the south here in the Southern Hemisphere. At the start of my trip, it looked a lot like a hybrid of Southern California, so San Diego, LA, and and Miami especially as I moved north from Brisbane to the Gold Coast. Very Southern California feel, and you mixed in the the skyscrapers on the beach, it felt like Miami with better, less humid weather because it it is winter here right now, so it made it very, very pleasant. That's where I swam in the ocean. But as I've worked my way further north, it is now giving a distinctly California vibe. It's windier, it's cooler, and it is more dramatic when it comes to the topography. This reminds me a lot, to be honest, of Point Reyes in Marin County. And Byron Bay reminded me of a quaint Northern California beach town, probably with a little bit more Southern California flavor. So, that's that very, very unique Australian mix. I had an awesome, awesome steak sandwich, by the way, in Byron Bay. We'll see what's for dinner. Could add that to this video when I do edit it. So, now, you know, I've I've organized this trip so that, obviously, Melbourne is next. That's where the 49ers play the Rams. That city has been compared to San Francisco. I know that Americans always try to find an American equivalent, so we shall see. Obviously, we're going further south, so it's going to be much cooler there. I've had to bring many different types of clothes for this trip because we started off in 80° weather, and we're probably going to be down to the 50s at at some point of this trip. And then, Sydney, the biggest city in Australia, that's going to be the grand finale of the Australia portion of this trip. So, we take a look at the sunset right here underneath the Cape Byron Lighthouse. How about another graphic for you? Take a Take a look at this. I I've talked about pressure and the ability to administer it. And, you know, some of the other videos I've been doing because of the 49ers edge rusher situation, been talking a lot about Raheem Morris and his propensity to manufacture pressure. This is last year. Scheme blitz rate is on the x-axis. EPA per play on scheme blitz rate, so better for the defense if you're higher. It's a lower EPA is on the y-axis. So, you can see the 49ers neither blitzed a lot nor were they effective blitzing. They're in the bottom left quadrant. Raheem Morris though was with the Falcons last year. They blitzed a lot, only less than the Minnesota Vikings and Brian Flores. And they were in the upper right quadrant. More effective, more frequent with the blitzes for the Atlanta Falcons. So, what do I expect? I expect more frequent and more effective blitzes for the 49ers. And that's something that you know, Matthew Stafford played against Raheem Morris last year and he lost to him. The Falcons beat the Rams on Monday night football. They created some real issues for Matthew Stafford. they'll study that. Sean McVay will definitely study that, but Morris is now working with different personnel. He's been a chameleon over his time in the NFL and you know, just remember the original truth that I told you here, the 49ers have a better quarterback when it comes to handling pressure. The data doesn't lie. And in week one, when you could probably throw some unpredictable pressure out there with new personnel, new setting, not a lot of, you know, fully organic tape to watch, could be a big advantage for the 49ers.
